{{short description|Construction on any polygon that yields a regular polygon with the same number of sides}}
In [[geometry]], the '''Petr–Douglas–Neumann theorem''' (or the '''PDN-theorem''') is a result concerning arbitrary [[plane (geometry)|planar]] [[polygon]]s. The theorem asserts that a certain [[algorithm|procedure]] when applied to an arbitrary polygon always yields a [[regular polygon]] having the same number of sides as the initial polygon. The theorem was first published by [[Karel Petr]] (1868–1950) of [[Prague]] in 1905 (in Czech)<ref>{{cite journal | last=Petr | first=Karel | title=O jedné větě pro mnohoúhelníky rovinné | trans-title = On a theorem for the plane polygons | journal=Časopis pro pěstování matematiky a fysiky | volume=034 | issue=2 | date=1905 | issn=1802-114X | doi=10.21136/CPMF.1905.120936 | pages=166–172 | language=cs| doi-access=free }}</ref> and in 1908 (in German).<ref>{{cite journal|last=K. Petr|title=Ein Satz über Vielecke|journal=Arch. Math. Phys.|year=1908|volume=13|pages=29–31}}</ref><ref name=Gray/> It was independently rediscovered by [[Jesse Douglas]] (1897–1965) in 1940<ref name=Douglas>{{cite journal|last=Douglas|first=Jesse|title=On linear polygon transformations|journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society|year=1940|volume=46|issue=6|pages=551–561|url=https://www.ams.org/journals/bull/1940-46-06/S0002-9904-1940-07259-3/S0002-9904-1940-07259-3.pdf|accessdate=7 May 2012|doi=10.1090/s0002-9904-1940-07259-3|doi-access=free}}</ref> and also by [[Bernhard Neumann|B H Neumann]] (1909–2002) in 1941.<ref name=Gray/><ref>{{cite journal|last=B H Neumann|title=Some remarks on polygons|journal=Journal of the London Mathematical Society |year=1941|volume=s1-16|issue=4 |pages=230–245|doi=10.1112/jlms/s1-16.4.230}}</ref>  The naming of the theorem as ''Petr–Douglas–Neumann theorem'', or as the ''PDN-theorem'' for short,  is due to Stephen B Gray.<ref name=Gray/> It has also been called '''Douglas's theorem''', the '''Douglas–Neumann theorem''', the '''Napoleon–Douglas–Neumann theorem'''  and '''Petr's theorem'''.<ref name=Gray/>

The PDN-theorem is a generalisation of [[Napoleon's theorem]], which corresponds to the case of [[triangle]]s, and [[van Aubel's theorem]] which corresponds to the case of [[quadrilateral]]s.

==Statement of the theorem==
The Petr–Douglas–Neumann theorem asserts the following.<ref name=Douglas/><ref>{{cite web|author1=van Lamoen, Floor  |author2=Weisstein, Eric W.|title=Petr–Neumann–Douglas Theorem.|url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/Petr-Neumann-DouglasTheorem.html|publisher=From MathWorld—A Wolfram Web Resource|accessdate=8 May 2012}}</ref>

:''If isosceles triangles with apex angles 2kπ/n, for an integer k with 1 ≤ k ≤ n − 2 are erected on the sides of an arbitrary n-gon A<sub>0</sub>, whose apices are the vertices of a new n-gon A<sub>1</sub>, and if this process is repeated n-2 times, but with a different value of k for the n-gon formed from the free apices of these triangles at each step, until all values 1 ≤ k ≤ n − 2 have been used (in arbitrary order), to form a sequence A<sub>1</sub>, A<sub>2</sub>, ... A<sub>n-2</sub>, of n-gons, their centroids all coincide with the centroid of A<sub>0</sub>, and the last one, A<sub>n−2</sub> is a regular n-gon ''.{{efn|Here, "centroid" is meant the [[vertex centroid]].}}

==Specialisation to triangles==

[[File:PDNTheoremForTriangle.svg|thumb|250px|Diagram illustrating the fact that Napoleon's theorem is a special case of Petr–Douglas–Neumann theorem.]] 
In the case of triangles, the value of ''n'' is 3 and that of ''n''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;2 is 1. Hence there is only one possible value for ''k'', namely 1. The specialisation of the  theorem to triangles  asserts that the triangle A<sub>1</sub> is a regular 3-gon, that is, an equilateral triangle.

A<sub>1</sub> is formed by the apices of the isosceles triangles with apex angle 2π/3 erected over the sides of the triangle A<sub>0</sub>. The vertices of A<sub>1</sub> are the centers of equilateral triangles erected over the sides of triangle A<sub>0</sub>. Thus the specialisation of the PDN theorem to a triangle can be formulated as follows:

:''If equilateral triangles are erected over the sides of any triangle, then the triangle formed by the centers of the three equilateral triangles is equilateral.''

The last statement is the assertion of the [[Napoleon's theorem]].

==Specialisation to quadrilaterals==

In the case of [[quadrilateral]]s, the value of ''n'' is 4 and that  of ''n''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;2 is&nbsp;2. There are two possible values for ''k'', namely 1 and 2, and so two possible apex angles, namely:

:(2×1×π)/4 = π/2 = 90° ( corresponding to ''k'' = 1 )
:(2×2×π)/4 = π = 180° ( corresponding to ''k'' = 2 ).

According to the PDN-theorem the quadrilateral A<sub>2</sub> is a regular 4-gon, that is, a [[Square (geometry)|square]]. The two-stage process yielding the square A<sub>2</sub> can be carried out in two different ways. (The apex ''Z'' of an [[isosceles triangle]] with apex angle π erected over a line segment ''XY'' is  the [[midpoint]] of the line segment ''XY''.)

===Construct A<sub>1</sub> using apex angle π/2 and then A<sub>2</sub> with apex angle π.===

In this case the [[vertex (geometry)|vertices]] of A<sub>1</sub> are the free apices of [[isosceles triangle]]s with apex angles π/2 erected over the sides of the quadrilateral A<sub>0</sub>. The vertices of the quadrilateral A<sub>2</sub> are the [[midpoint]]s of the sides of the quadrilateral A<sub>1</sub>. By the PDN theorem, A<sub>2</sub> is a square.

The vertices of the quadrilateral A<sub>1</sub> are the centers of squares erected over the sides of the quadrilateral A<sub>0</sub>. The assertion that quadrilateral A<sub>2</sub> is a square is equivalent to the assertion that the [[diagonal]]s of A<sub>1</sub> are equal and [[perpendicular]] to each other. The latter assertion is the content of [[van Aubel's theorem]].

Thus [[van Aubel's theorem]] is a special case of the PDN-theorem.

===Construct A<sub>1</sub> using apex angle π and then A<sub>2</sub> with apex angle π/2.===

In this case the vertices of A<sub>1</sub> are the [[midpoint]]s of the sides of the quadrilateral A<sub>0</sub>  and those of A<sub>2</sub> are the apices of the triangles with apex angles π/2 erected over the sides of A<sub>1</sub>. The PDN-theorem asserts that A<sub>2</sub> is a square in this case also.

==Specialisation to pentagons==
[[File:PDN Theorem For Pentagon.svg|thumb|300px|Diagram illustrating Petr–Douglas–Neumann theorem as applied to a pentagon. The pentagon ''A''<sub>0</sub> is ''ABCDE''. ''A''<sub>1</sub> ( = ''FGHIJ'' ) is constructed with apex angle 72°, ''A''<sub>2</sub> ( = ''KLMNO'' ) with apex angle 144° and ''A''<sub>3</sub> ( = ''PQRST'' ) with apex angle 216°.]]
In the case of [[pentagon]]s, we have ''n'' = 5 and ''n''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;2 =&nbsp;3. So there are three possible values for ''k'', namely 1, 2 and 3, and hence three possible apex angles for isosceles triangles:

:(2×1×π)/5 = 2π/5 = 72°
:(2×2×π)/5 = 4π/5 = 144°
:(2×3×π)/5 = 6π/5 = 216°

According to the PDN-theorem, A<sub>3</sub> is a [[regular pentagon]]. The three-stage process leading to the construction of the regular pentagon A<sub>3</sub> can be performed in six different ways depending on the order in which the apex angles are selected for the construction of the isosceles triangles. 
:

|-

|-
| 1 || 72° || 144° || 216°
|-
| 2 || 72° || 216° || 144°
|-
| 3 || 144° || 72° || 216°
|-
| 4 || 144° || 216° || 72°
|-
| 5 || 216° || 72°  || 144°
|-
| 6 || 216° || 144° || 72° 
|}

==Proof of the theorem==

The theorem can be proved using some elementary concepts from [[linear algebra]].<ref name=Gray>{{cite journal|last=Stephen B. Gray|title=Generalizing the Petr–Douglas–Neumann Theorem on ''n''-gons|journal=American Mathematical Monthly|volume=110|issue=3|pages=210–227|url=https://www.experimentalmath.info/workshop2004/gray-article.pdf|accessdate=8 May 2012|doi=10.2307/3647935|jstor=3647935|year=2003|citeseerx=10.1.1.605.2676}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Omar Antolín Camarena|title=The Petr–Neumann–Douglas theorem through linear algebra|url=https://www.matem.unam.mx/~omar/notes/petr.html|accessdate=10 Jan 2018}}</ref>

The proof begins by encoding an ''n''-gon by a list of complex numbers representing the vertices of the ''n''-gon. This list can be thought of as a vector in the ''n''-dimensional complex linear space C<sup>n</sup>.  Take an ''n''-gon ''A'' and  let it be represented by the complex vector

:''A'' = ( ''a''<sub>1</sub>, ''a''<sub>2</sub>, ... , ''a''<sub>''n''</sub> ).

Let the polygon  ''B'' be formed by the free vertices of similar triangles built on the sides of ''A'' and let it be represented by the complex vector

:''B'' = ( ''b''<sub>1</sub>, ''b''<sub>2</sub>, ... , ''b''<sub>''n''</sub> ).

Then we have

:α( ''a''<sub>''r''</sub> &minus; ''b''<sub>''r''</sub> )  =  ''a''<sub>''r''+1</sub> &minus; ''b''<sub>''r''</sub>, where α = exp( ''i'' θ ) for some θ (here ''i'' is the square root of&nbsp;&minus;1).

This yields the following expression to compute the ''b''<sub>r</sub> ' s:

:''b''<sub>''r''</sub> = (1−α)<sup>−1</sup> ( ''a''<sub>''r''+1</sub> − α''a''<sub>''r''</sub> ).

In terms of the linear operator ''S'' : C<sup>n</sup> → C<sup>n</sup> that cyclically permutes the coordinates one place, we have 
:''B'' = (1−α)<sup>−1</sup>( ''S'' − α''I'' )''A'',  where ''I'' is the [[identity matrix]].

This means that the polygon ''A''<sub>j+1</sub>
obtained at the ''j''the step is related to the preceding one ''A''<sub>j</sub> by

: ''A''<sub>j+1</sub> '' = ( 1 − ω<sup>σ<sub>j</sub></sup> )<sup>−1</sup>( ''S'' − ω<sup>σ<sub>j</sub></sup> ''I'' ) ''A''<sub>j</sub> '',

where ω = exp( 2π''i''/''n'' ) is the ''n''th primitive [[root of unity]] and ''σ<sub>j</sub>'' is the ''j''th term of a permutation ''σ'' of the integer sequence ''(1,..., n-2)''.

The last polygon in the sequence, ''A''<sub>''n''−2</sub>, which we need to show is regular, is thus obtained from ''A''<sub>0</sub> by applying the composition of all the following operators:

: ( 1 − ω<sup>''j''</sup> )<sup>−1</sup>( ''S'' − ω<sup>j</sup> ''I'' ) for ''j'' = 1, 2, ... , ''n'' − 2 . 

(These factors commute, since they are all polynomials in the same operator ''S'', so the ordering of the product does not depend on the choice of the permutation ''σ''.)

A polygon ''P'' = ( ''p''<sub>1</sub>, ''p''<sub>2</sub>, ..., ''p''<sub>''n''</sub> ) is a regular ''n''-gon if each side of ''P''  is obtained from the next by rotating through an angle of 2π/''n'', that is, if 
: ''p''<sub>''r'' + 1</sub> − ''p''<sub>''r''</sub> = ω( ''p''<sub>''r'' + 2</sub> − ''p''<sub>''r'' + 1</sub> ).
This condition can be formulated in terms of S as follows:

:( ''S'' − ''I'' )( ''I'' − ω''S'' ) ''P'' = 0.

Or equivalently as

:( ''S'' − ''I'' )( ''S'' &minus; ω<sup>''n'' &minus; 1</sup> ''I'' ) ''P'' = 0, since ω<sup>''n''</sup> = 1.

The main result of the Petr–Douglas–Neumann theorem now follows from the following computations.

:( ''S'' − ''I'' )( ''S'' &minus; ω<sup>''n'' &minus; 1</sup> ''I'' ) ''A''<sub>''n'' &minus; 2</sub>
:: = ( ''S'' − ''I'' )( ''S'' &minus; ω<sup>''n'' &minus; 1</sup> ''I'' )  ( 1 − ω )<sup>−1</sup> ( ''S'' &minus;  ω ''I'' ) ( 1 − ω<sup>2</sup> )<sup>−1</sup> ( ''S'' &minus;  ω<sup>2</sup> ''I'' ) ... ( 1 − ω<sup>''n'' &minus; 2</sup> )<sup>−1</sup> ( ''S'' &minus;  ω<sup>''n'' &minus; 2</sup> ''I'' ) ''A''<sub>0</sub>
:: = ( 1 − ω )<sup>−1</sup>( 1 − ω<sup>2</sup> )<sup>−1</sup> ... ( 1 − ω<sup>''n'' &minus; 2</sup> )<sup>−1</sup> ( ''S'' &minus; ''I'' ) ( ''S'' &minus; ω ''I'' ) ( ''S'' &minus; ω<sup>2</sup> ''I'' ) ... ( ''S'' &minus; ω<sup>''n'' &minus; 1</sup> ''I'')''A''<sub>0</sub>
:: = ( 1 − ω )<sup>−1</sup>( 1 − ω<sup>2</sup> )<sup>−1</sup> ... ( 1 − ω<sup>''n'' &minus; 2</sup> )<sup>−1</sup> ( ''S''<sup>''n''</sup> &minus; ''I'' ) ''A''<sub>0</sub>
:: = 0, since ''S''<sup>''n''</sup> = ''I''.

To show that all the  centroids are equal, we note
that the centroid ''c<sub>A</sub>'' of any n-gon is obtained by averagining all the vertices. This means that, viewing ''A'' as an ''n''-component vector, its centroid is given by taking its scalar product
 
:''c<sub>A</sub>''= ''(E , A)''

with the vector ''E:=(1/n) (1, 1, ..., 1)'' .
Taking the scalar product of both sides of the equation
: ''A''<sub>j+1</sub> '' = ( 1 − ω<sup>σ<sub>j</sub></sup> )<sup>−1</sup>( ''S'' − ω<sup>σ<sub>j</sub></sup> ''I'' ) ''A''<sub>j</sub> '',

with ''E'', and noting that ''E'' is invariant under the [[cyclic permutation]] operator ''S'', we obtain

: ''c<sub>A<sub>j+1</sub></sub> ''= (E, ''A<sub>j+1</sub>'') = ( 1 − ω<sup>σ<sub>j</sub></sup> )<sup>−1</sup> ( 1 − ω<sup>σ<sub>j</sub></sup> )(E, ''A<sub>j</sub>'') = (E, ''A<sub>j</sub>'') =  ''c<sub>A<sub>j</sub></sub> '',

so all the centroids are equal.
